title: memory-pressure-span-analysis-and-mitigation-proposal
content:
Summary:

This is a working incident review and runbook proposal for a class of memory-pressure incidents observed across serving-runtime hosts during late-November and January test windows. Symptoms: elevated host memory RSS, progressive OOM kills in the runtime process, and a correlated spike in active KV cache entries and continuous-batching queue depth. We believe a behavioral regression in the batching scheduler + a subtle per-tenant KV cache accounting drift created long-lived, low-throughput batches that amplified memory retention and prevented timely eviction.

Why this doc exists (notes to self):
- capture a repeatable triage path for on-call engineers
- propose pragmatic mitigations that are low-risk for immediate rollout
- list telemetry + queries to quickly confirm hypotheses in future incidents
- surface experiments to validate in staging before wider rollout

Impact observed (examples):
- 2025-11-18 02:13 UTC: 8 hosts in us-west-2 serving-runtime pool reported OOM kills over 18 min; customer-facing latency increased 3x for long-context requests, error rate 5% for generation endpoints
- 2026-01-22 14:40 UTC: controlled regression test triggered similar memory rise in dedicated capacity (canary pool), causing one host to cross the kill threshold after 24 minutes
- In both cases, garbage collection / allocator activity (jemalloc stats) did not indicate a single giant allocation — memory climbed via many small-ish allocations held in KV caches and batching queues

High-level hypothesis (short):
1) A scheduler change (PR: serving-runtime#2287) unintentionally increased max batch wait time for a subset of request shapes, causing longer-lived batch objects to accumulate.
2) Longer-lived batches keep references to per-request KV cache frames (prefix caches + tokenized tensors), preventing eviction heuristics from lowering memory pressure.
3) The KV cache accounting code (per-host counters) drifts under high concurrency because some eviction callbacks are dropped on race paths; thus reported freeable memory is overstated.

Evidence collected:
- heap+rss timeline traces from host-1234 (us-west-2) show steady +1.2GB/hour increase over the incident window; no single allocation spike in jemalloc stats.
- stack samples taken immediately before OOM show high probability in scheduler::flush_batch and kv_cache::record_access (sampling: 18/50 backtraces).
- continuous-batching queue depth metrics (cb_queue_depth{shape="long-context"}) rose from baseline ~3 to peaks of ~120 for affected hosts.
- eviction callback failure logs: small but non-zero count of TTL eviction callbacks failing due to lock-timeout exceptions in the same interval.
- canary reproduction: toggling scheduler heuristics (reduce max_wait_ms from 50->20) prevented memory growth in a 2-hour synthetic load run.

Immediate mitigations (fast, low-risk):
- Hotfix A (safe): Reduce scheduler max batch wait threshold for long-context shapes from 50ms to 20ms via remote config override. Rollout as a canary to 5% of serving hosts in each region. Rationale: shorter-lived batches reduce KV retention time.
- Hotfix B (surgical): Enable aggressive per-host kv-cache eviction tracing (DEBUG) to gather stack traces for failed evictions; toggled for affected hosts only.
- Hotfix C (protective): Add a temporary host-level memory circuit that rejects new large-context requests when host RSS > 85% of container limit, returning 429 with a diagnostic header. This prevents OOM kills while preserving other traffic.

Proposed runbook (for on-call):
1) Triage initial alert: "serving-runtime OOMs" pager -> gather host list, region, start_time.
2) Confirm symptoms: check host RSS vs container limit, number of OOM kills in last 30m, and cb_queue_depth per host. PromQL queries below.
3) If cb_queue_depth > 50 on multiple hosts: immediately flip Hotfix A via runtime-config and monitor 5m rolling windows.
4) If host-level memory is climbing > 200MB / 10m and scheduler change rollback not possible: trigger Hotfix C on affected hosts to shed large-context requests.
5) Collect artifacts: jemalloc stats, /proc/smaps, pprof heap profile if safe, and a 30s flame sample. Upload to incident channel and attach to JIRA ticket.
6) Keep on-call SRE and serving-runtime engineer looped until memory stabilizes for 1 hour post-mitigation.

Prometheus / Logging queries (quick copyable):
- Hosts with rising RSS (last 30m):
  increase(container_memory_rss_bytes{job="serving-runtime"}[30m]) > 2e8
- Current cb queue depth (grouped by host, shape):
  max_over_time(cb_queue_depth[5m]) by (host, shape)
- Eviction callback failure count:
  increase(kv_cache_eviction_fail_total[15m]) by (host)
- Requests rejected by memory circuit: counter memory_shed_rejects_total{host}

Suggested on-call commands (notes):
- pprof: sudo /usr/local/bin/pprof --http=:6060 /var/log/pprof/heap_$(date +%s).pb
- jemalloc stats: echo "stats" > /proc/$(pidof serving-runtime)/fd/0 (wrap carefully)
- quick smaps diff: sudo smem -k -P serving-runtime | head -n 40

Longer-term fixes and experiments:
- Fix A (code): Harden kv_cache eviction to ensure eviction callbacks run under contention (rework lock ordering, ensure callback completion tracked even under cancel paths). This needs a thorough concurrency review and unit+stress tests. Owner: Claire Nguyen.
- Fix B (scheduler): Revisit batching heuristics to prefer batch size over wait-time for long-context shapes; add microbenchmarks that exercise skewed shape distributions. Owner: Miguel Torres.
- Fix C (accounting): Add a periodic consistency check that compares per-host tracked freeable memory to observed allocator freeable statistics and logs divergence > 10%. If divergence detected, trigger a local cache compaction and alert. Owner: eng-sre team.
- Experiment: instrument per-batch lifetime histogram (labels: shape, host, batch_size) and run in staging for 72 hours with synthetic load skewed to long-context flows. Goal: correlate batch lifetime with memory retention and eviction timing.

Dashboard + alert tuning recommendations:
- New panel: batch_lifetime_p50/p95 by shape. Alert if p95 > 250ms for long-context shapes.
- Adjust existing OOM policy: treat OOM-kill spikes across >5 hosts in 15m as P1; previously threshold was 10 hosts — too lenient for dedicated pools.
- Add 'memory-accounting-drift' alert: per-host (tracked_freeable - allocator_freeable) > 10% for 10m.

Security / customer impact notes:
- No evidence of data leakage; KV cache entries are ephemeral and not stored externally.
- Customers on dedicated pools may see transient 429s if Hotfix C is enabled, document in status page and PSR ticket.

Next steps (owners & ETA):
- Short-term (1 week): rollout Hotfix A to production 100% if canary shows <5% latency impact. Owner: Miguel.
- Medium-term (3 weeks): land Fix A (kv eviction hardening) behind feature flag; run multi-tenant stress tests. Owner: Claire.
- Long-term (8–12 weeks): scheduler rework + new accounting checks + dashboard bake. Owner: SRE eng lead.

Open questions / unresolved: 
- Why did eviction callbacks fail under contention? Need trace-level reproduction.
- Is there any interaction with quantization memory paths that hold GPU pinned buffers? We saw only host RSS increases but confirm via GPU telemetry.
- Are there specific tenants or request patterns (client libs) that produce many small allocations and hold them in user-facing response structures longer than necessary?

Appendix: useful links and snippets
- Repro harness for synthetic load (staging): scripts/repro/long_context_skew.sh (PR link in artifacts)
- Slack thread: https://slack.redwood.com/archives/C012AB3CD/thread-1648392
- Related PR: github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/2287 (scheduler change landed Oct)

Notes to on-call: try to be conservative with pprof/dumps on production hosts — prefer sampling and short snapshots. If in doubt, reach out to Claire or Miguel before an intrusive dump.

End of draft.

(If you are reading this: add reproduction artifacts and exact pprof filenames to the ticket before closing.)
